content: Anionic acid is not considered an additional effective agent for tuberculosis (TB) treatment and should not be used independently of imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on TB management in children and adolescents, the eligibility criteria for treatment regimens for children with confirmed multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) are the same as those for adolescents and adults.g., cavities or bilateral disease on chest X-ray). Additionally, the presence of specific genetic mutations (inhA promoter region and katG gene) suggests that high-dose isoniazid and thioamides are ineffective. Children diagnosed with rifampicin resistance alone, without further drug susceptibility testing (DST), can be treated with bedaquiline-containing regimens at the discretion of the treating clinician. The standardized all-oral bedaquiline-containing shorter regimen includes medicines such as bedaquiline, high-dose isoniazid, ethionamide/prothionamide, levofloxacin, clofazimine, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. If smear or culture results remain positive after four months of treatment, the initial phase may be extended up to six months. For children without bacteriological confirmation or those unable to produce a specimen but showing clinical improvement, treatment can transition to the continuation phase after four months, with bedaquiline continued for six months. The use of bedaquiline in children has been recommended since 2019 for those over six years of age, with updated dosing guidelines for younger children based on limited data. The WHO has also announced updates to treatment regimens, including a nine-month all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen with linezolid instead of ethionamide. For children with severe disease or limited treatment options, individualized regimens should include at least four effective medicines, with bedaquiline and linezolid prioritized. Delamanid may be added if fluoroquinolone resistance or severe disease is suspected. Injectable agents like amikacin and streptomycin are not recommended for children due to the risk of permanent hearing loss. For children with TB meningitis (TBM), treatment regimens should include medicines with good cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) penetration, such as fluoroquinolones, linezolid, cycloserine, and ethionamide. Longer durations of linezolid may be necessary for TBM due to its efficacy in penetrating the CSF. Most other forms of extrapulmonary MDR/RR-TB can be treated similarly to pulmonary TB, with longer regimens required for severe cases like osteoarticular TB. Monitoring during treatment is essential to assess response, identify treatment failure, and manage adverse effects. Clinical improvement, weight gain, and radiographic changes are key indicators of treatment success. Adverse effects of TB medicines vary by drug class, with common side effects including gastrointestinal disturbances, liver dysfunction, QT interval prolongation, and myelosuppression. For children living with HIV, antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens should avoid efavirenz due to its interaction with bedaquiline, while integrase inhibitors like dolutegravir are preferred. Child-friendly formulations of second-line TB medicines, such as dispersible tablets, are strongly recommended to facilitate administration. If unavailable, adult formulations can be manipulated (e.g., crushed or dissolved) for pediatric use. Medicines like bedaquiline and delamanid have been shown to retain bioavailability when prepared as suspensions or dissolved in water, making them suitable for children who cannot swallow tablets. Regular monitoring of children on MDR/RR-TB treatment includes clinical, radiological, and microbiological assessments. Weight and growth should be tracked monthly, and adherence to treatment should be evaluated. Any signs of treatment failure, such as worsening symptoms or weight loss, should prompt further investigation, including follow-up cultures and DST.
